summary: This informational memo lists requirements for a protocol that carries authentication for network access (PANA). Today the mechanisms for authenticating to a network depend on the access technology, so a single IP-based protocol would work across many link types.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4058 lists requirements for the Protocol for Carrying Authentication for Network Access (PANA). It would carry existing authentication information between a device and an access network across different link technologies.

questions: protocol for carrying authentication for network access
pana requirements for network access authentication
what is an enforcement point in pana
subtitle: Requirements for carrying network-access authentication across different link technologies.

tldr.problem: Existing network-access authentication methods are tied to particular access links or topologies. The PANA work needed requirements for a method that could operate over any link layer supporting IP.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes PANA as a carrier for existing authentication methods, such as EAP, between a client and an agent in the access network; it does not define a new authentication method.
tldr.outcome: The requirements limit the scope of PANA design work. They cover authentication, network behavior, management, congestion control and security without specifying the protocol itself.

facts.label: Client addressing
facts.value: An IP address is required before PANA runs

today: RFC 4058 is an Informational requirements document published in May 2005. It specifies no protocol and the unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why a Link-Independent Carrier Is Needed
sections.content:
Network access may require a provider to authenticate and authorize a device. The methods available at the time were tied to specific access types: 802.1X applies to IEEE 802 links, while PPP applies to point-to-point links. Operators using other access arrangements could need ad-hoc solutions.

PANA is intended as a network-layer carrier for authentication payloads between a host and an agent in the access network. It is meant to work independently of the underlying access technology, not to invent new security protocols or key-management methods.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC describes requirements for carrying authentication data over the Internet across different kinds of access links. The planned protocol carries existing security methods instead of replacing them.

sections.title: Client, Agent and Enforcement Point
sections.content:
The PANA Client (PaC) runs on the host and provides credentials. The PANA Authentication Agent (PAA) runs on the access-network side, checks those credentials, and grants network access to the device identified by a Device Identifier (DI).

An Enforcement Point (EP) applies per-packet filters to a client's traffic. The PAA may be separate from the EP; if so, another secure protocol must carry the authorization information needed by the enforcement points.
sections.plainLanguage: The device supplies credentials to an agent in the access network. A network point then applies packet rules to that device after access is approved.

sections.title: Authentication and Authorization Requirements
sections.content:
PANA must support client authentication and grant network access to the device, rather than separately authorizing each person who uses it. It must act as a carrier for existing security protocols; EAP is named as a candidate. The client and agent must be capable of mutual authentication, periodic and on-demand re-authentication, and two independent authentication operations for one client.

PANA does not assign the client's IP address, provide accounting, or define fine-grained authorization for individual services. The client must already have an IP address before running PANA. A separate secure-association protocol may use EAP key material to establish IPsec protection for data traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: The planned protocol carries an existing identity check and can repeat it when needed. It does not assign an Internet address or decide access to each individual service.

sections.title: Network Operation and Security
sections.content:
The PAA and client must be exactly one IP hop apart, with no IP router between them, and PANA must provide a way for a client to discover the PAA. The protocol must support clients with multiple interfaces and networks with multiple routers, and it must work with both IPv4 and IPv6.

PANA must not assume a secure channel and must protect against replay and denial-of-service attacks, including blind masquerade using spoofed IP addresses. It must provide congestion control. The RFC's usage examples place the PAA with the enforcement point, the access router, both, or separately from them.
sections.plainLanguage: The device and agent must be separated by one Internet routing step, and the device must be able to find the agent. The protocol must work with both major Internet address versions and protect exchanges from replay, fakes and overload.
